extracted.intended_audience: researchers in psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and behavioural science studying laughter, humour and vocal communication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and synthesis for studying and interpreting human laughter (its production, perception, contagion and development), with emphasis on Provine's observational/naturalistic methods and comparative perspectives. Useful for designing studies, analysing acoustic/behavioural data, and interpreting social and evolutionary functions of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological validity / naturalistic observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter needs to be studied in ecologically valid environments; many important observations come from natural interactions rather than laboratory elicitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observational methods (Provine's approach, analogous to Jane Goodall's primate studies). Avoid assuming lab-induced laughter is representative; capture authentic recordings (e.g. live broadcasts) and contextual information. Anti-pattern: forcing participants to 'laugh on command' in sterile lab settings without social context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish spontaneous versus communicative laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate spontaneous (involuntary) laughter from communicative (volitional) laughter—listeners can often tell them apart, and they are likely controlled by different neural systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design analyses and interpretations around these categories: spontaneous laughter may reflect midline involuntary vocalization networks and disrupt speech, while communicative laughter may involve volitional speech motor networks and be precisely timed in conversation. Consider mixed forms in natural data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and quantify behavioural contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is highly behaviourally contagious; many laughter episodes occur simply because someone else laughed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess contagion by examining temporal sequences, who laughs first, and social relationship effects (familiarity increases contagion). Use recorded stimuli and contagion paradigms (recorded laughter can elicit laughter). Note developmental facts: babies do not initially show contagious laughter—it is learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social context and interpersonal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Social context strongly modulates laughter: people are far more likely to laugh in the presence of others, and contagion is stronger among acquaintances than strangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect information on social setting, group composition, and relationship quality. Expect large effects of social facilitation; include measures of loneliness, trait empathy, or relationship status as covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic and prosodic analysis (oscillogram, pitch, spectral shape)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use acoustic measures (oscillograms, pitch profiles, spectral analyses) to characterise laughter and its interaction with speech (e.g. raised pitch when smiling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools such as Praat can estimate pitch and display oscillograms. Examine pitch changes, wheezing laughs, timing of exhalations, and spectral shifts due to smiling. Report annotated transcripts aligned with acoustic plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with speech: dysfluency and breathing disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can disrupt speech production (pauses, repetitions, dysfluency) and breathing; automatic/involuntary laughter may overwhelm verbal control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code and quantify speech interruptions, pauses, repetitions and respiratory effects when laughter occurs. Interpret prolonged or uncontrollable laughter as evidence of involuntary systems dominating production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental trajectory and infant laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter emerges early in infancy and its elicitors shift over development from tactile to acoustic/social/visual actions; contagious laughter is learned over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include age-stratified analyses and consider which eliciting actions (tickling, lip popping, peek-a-boo) are relevant at different ages. Use longitudinal or diary methods to track acquisition of contagious responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and population heterogeneity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural/historical heterogeneity predicts differences in smiling and laughing frequency and the accuracy of decoding laughter/colaughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cross-cultural sampling or measures of population migration history; expect variation in frequency, decoding accuracy and reliance on non-verbal cues. Report how social norms may shape laughter expression and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative and evolutionary perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare human laughter to play vocalizations and tickling-related vocalizations in other animals, but be cautious: purely contagious laughter appears uniquely human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative data (apes, rats, other mammals) to infer evolutionary continuity and discontinuity. Note contexts where other species produce laughter-like sounds (tickling, play) and limitations in their contagious responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is not synonymous with humour—functional interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most laughter in conversation is not tied to jokes; laughter often signals affiliation, agreement, affection, or understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting laughter episodes, code for apparent intent (humorous vs affiliative vs regulatory). Avoid assuming laughter necessarily indexes amusement; consider alternative social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diary and time-of-day / physiological-state measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Diaries reveal that laughter, smiling and talking are much more common socially and show time-of-day effects (attenuated after sleep), implicating physiological states like sleep inertia and cortisol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate time-of-day, sleep/wake measures, and physiological indices when possible. Expect reduced laughter immediately after sleep and modulation by anxiety or anxiolytics (e.g. alcohol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural/anatomical distinctions in laughter control
rubrics_metrics.description: Different neural pathways likely underlie involuntary vs volitional laughter (midline vocalization network vs volitional speech motor network); two neural networks for laughter are implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies that consider neural substrates (neuroimaging, lesion studies) and interpret behavioural data in light of possible dual-control systems. Be cautious inferring control from behaviour alone—use converging neural evidence where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental stimuli and perception tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptual experiments can test listeners' ability to judge authenticity, closeness, identity, and funniness from laughter and colaughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled playback of spontaneous vs posed laughs, measure ratings of funniness/authenticity/affiliation, and assess the modulatory effect of added laughter on humour ratings (e.g. bad jokes judged funnier when followed by spontaneous laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting practices: annotated transcripts, provenance and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide annotated transcripts, audio provenance (links/archives), and acoustic plots to contextualise analyses of naturalistic laughter episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include timestamps, speaker labels, acoustic figures (pitch, oscillogram), and source citations to allow replication and interpretation. Avoid presenting audio clips without contextual transcriptions or acoustic annotation.
